Although the temporal resolution of fNIRS is lower than that of EEG, fNIRS uses an infant-friendly headset without any paste or gel and is a more portable system, which has better temporal resolution (10 Hz) than fMRI. fNIRS measures neuronal activity reflected in changes in concentrations of oxygenated (oxy-) Hb and deoxygenated (deoxy-) Hb and it has been used to identify various neurocognitive developmental processes in infants (Minagawa-Kawai et al., 2011; Gervain et al., 2011; Minagawa-Kawai et al., 2008). Such findings have elucidated the cerebral responses of infants to two spoken language components: phonemes and prosody (Sato et al., 2003; Arimitsu et al., 2011). Furthermore, fNIRS allows researchers to explore the functional connectivity between different brain areas by examining the hemodynamic responses to specific cognitive stimuli. This approach is particularly promising for studying how networks of brain regions interact to support higher cognitive functions, such as language and executive functioning, both of which are crucial for a child's later development (Lloyd-Fox et al., 2010; Minagawa-Kawai et al., 2011). As the technique continues to evolve, it holds considerable potential in refining our understanding of preterm brain development and identifying early biomarkers for neurodevelopmental disorders. Integrating fNIRS with other neuroimaging modalities, such as EEG, can provide a more comprehensive picture of the preterm infant brain's functional architecture, offering insights into the maturation of neural pathways that are not accessible through any one method alone.

Many Syrians have been crossing over to the Bekaa by land to seek refuge in Lebanon since the beginning of the conflict in their home country. The agricultural sector in the Bekaa provides them with opportunities for work since it has always relied on seasonal migrant workers from Syria (Habib et al., 2016). Today, the Bekaa has the highest concentration of Syrian refugees in the country (341,131 individuals) (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, 2019). Children from these communities work in agriculture, construction, and the informal sector (International Labour Organization, 2015). The Lebanese labor law prohibits children younger than 14 years of age from working (Government of Lebanon, 1946) but it has not served as an effective deterrent. In recent years, considerable attention has been directed towards innovative techniques and technologies that could potentially mitigate these challenges and enhance the efficacy of diffusion MRI. One promising avenue lies in the development of advanced reconstruction algorithms that capitalize on sparsity and redundancy in the data, thus enabling high-resolution imaging at much lower SNRs than traditionally deemed feasible (Lustig et al., 2007; Jung et al., 2009). Compressed sensing, for instance, has been instrumental in reducing acquisition times without sacrificing quality, offering a vital tool for high-resolution applications (He and Zhu, 2010; Lustig et al., 2008). By cleverly exploiting the sparsity present in the diffusion-weighted images, compressed sensing techniques can reconstruct high-fidelity images from highly undersampled k-space data, which has the potential to revolutionize diffusion MRI protocols in clinical

However, there are several ways to increase the SNR efficiency while maintaining whole-brain coverage. One approach is to acquire fewer slices in each volume but increase the total number of volumes (i.e. slice undersampling) (Engstrom and Skare, 2013). This strategy increases the TR and thus improves the SNR efficiency, but it comes at the cost of reducing the temporal resolution. Alternatively, one may use three-dimensional (3D) imaging, which enables a reduction in the number of slices per volume while preserving the temporal resolution (Chang et al., 2015). The most common form of 3D acquisition in diffusion MRI is isotropic voxel 3D EPI (Seton et al., 2012; Cauley et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2015; O'Muircheartaigh et al., 2015; Scherrer et al., 2015). The complexity and inaccessibility of passive margins mean that many questions remain unanswered. By what mechanism is lithospheric stretching accommodated? The current understanding of the tectonic architecture of the Central Mozambique margin underscores the need for further integrative research that combines geological, geophysical, and geochemical datasets. At the heart of this research lies the challenge of unraveling the interplay between extensional forces and magmatic processes that have shaped this continental margin over millions of years. One key focus of contemporary studies is on identifying the nature of the transitional crustal zones present in the region. These zones are thought to be comprised of both stretched continental crust and new, nascent oceanic crust, marking the gradual evolution from continental to oceanic domains. Recent advancements in seismic reflection techniques have begun to illuminate the complex layering and faulting patterns that characterize these transitional zones. Partial solar eclipses occur when the Moon is not directly between the Sun and the Earth, and only part of the Sun is blocked.
